As a general rule, as article (a/an/the) is used before a singular countable noun.
I saw a woman in the street.
I saw an elephant in the street.
I saw the dog in the street.
The article ‘an’ is used before a vowel, a consonant sounded like a vowel, or a silent h; as,
an ass, an enemy, an inkpot, an orange, an umbrella, an M.A., an hour, an honest man, an historical building etc.
The article ‘a’ is used before a consonant, before u sounded as yu, and before o sounded as wu; as,
a boy, a woman, a yard, a house, a hole;
a university, a unicorn, a useful thing, a European;
a one-rupee note, a one-eyed man, such a one.
The article ‘the’ is used –
When we speak of a particular person or thing, or one already referred to, or known to the speaker; as
The book you gave me is very useful.
I dislike the fellow.
Let us go to the club.
When a singular noun is meant to represent a whole class; as,
The lion is the king of beasts.
The rose is the sweetest of all flowers.
With names of books, rivers, seas, oceans, groups of islands, gulfs, and mountain ranges; as,
The Gita, the Vedas, the Bible, the Ramayana.
The Ganges, the Jamuna, the Brahmaputra, the Red Sea, the Indian Ocean, the West Indies, the Persian Gulf, the Himalayas.
Before the name of things which are unique; as,
the sky, the Earth, the Moon, the Sun, the sea, the ocean etc.
Before Superlatives; as,
He is the best boy in our class.
Before an adjective when the noun is understood; as
The rich should be kind to the poor.
The article ‘a/an’ is used–
in the sense of ‘one’; as,
Wait a minute.
A bird in hand is worth two in the bush.
I have a pen and an inkpot.
Twelve inches make a foot.
in the vague sense of ‘a certain’; as,
There was an old man in the street.
One evening a bagger came to my door.
to single out an individual as the representative of a class; as,
A pupil should obey his teacher.
A cow is a useful animal.
No article is used–
Before a noun used in its widest sense; as,
Man is mortal.
What kind of flower is it?
Before names of materials; as
Gold is a precious metal.

Before proper noun; as
Bombay is a big city.
Ashoka was a great king.
Before abstract nouns used in a general sense; as

An Adverb should be placed as near as possible to the word or words it modifies; as,
He had got almost to the top when the rope broke.
Adverbs of Time (always, never, often, sometimes, generally, rarely, seldom, just, etc.) are placed immediately in front of the main verb of the sentence; as,
They are placed after the verb ‘be’; as,
You are never to come late again.
Other common adverbs coming in this position are:
The adverb ‘only’ should be placed carefully in a sentence. As a general rule, ‘only’ should be placed immediately before the word it is meant to modify; as,
Only Jolim could tell the truth.
I praise him only when he works hard.
Two negatives destroy each other. Hence two negatives should not be used in the same sentence unless we wish to make an affirmative statement. We should say:
I could not find it anywhere (not nowhere).
I haven't any (not no) homework to do.
I can't see any (not no) grace in her.
Adjectives should not be used for Adverbs. We should say, for instance:
He returned more quickly (not quicker) than I expected.
He will pay heavily (not heavy) for his mistake.
We seldom or never (not ever) visit our relatives.
It seldom or never (not ever) rains in this month.
Note: ‘Seldom or never’ and ‘seldom if ever’ are both correct but ‘seldom or ever’ is incorrect.
‘Other than’ is used after a negative.
It is nothing else but (not else than) pride.
She had no close friends other than him.
‘Very’ is used with a Positive degree of Adjective.
‘Much’ is used with a Comparative degree of Adjective.
The Present Participle (V₁-ing) as an Adjective takes 'very' with it.
The Past Participle (V3) as an Adjective takes ‘much’ with it.
I am much worried about her.
She has a very charming face.
It is a much discussed topic.
Note: A few Past Participles take ‘very’ before them; as,
I am very pleased to hear this.
The adverb ‘too’ means ‘more than enough’. It should not be used in the sense of ‘very’ or ‘much’.
I am too pleased with you. 		(incorrect)
I am very pleased with you. 		(correct)
She is too interested in music. 	(incorrect)
She is much interested in music.	(correct)

‘Enough’ (as an adverb) is used after the word it qualifies.
He is too weak to walk.

The adverb ‘never’ can't be used with verbs indicating a special point of time.
